data.title: The Life of the Buddha
data.sourcePassage: Buddhism is based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, who lived approximately 2,500 years ago in what is now Nepal. He was born into a royal family and raised in great luxury, protected from the realities of suffering. When he ventured outside the palace, he encountered the Four Sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and finally a wandering holy man who appeared peaceful despite living without wealth. These encounters shattered his worldview. Deeply troubled by what he had seen, Siddhartha left his palace, wife, and child in search of the truth about suffering. He tried extreme asceticism — nearly starving himself — but rejected this path and chose instead the Middle Way between indulgence and self-denial. After 49 days of deep meditation under a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, he achieved enlightenment — a profound awakening and understanding of suffering and liberation. From this point he was called the Buddha, meaning 'Awakened One'. He spent the next 45 years teaching the Dharma before his death, known as parinirvana.

data.title: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
data.sourcePassage: The Four Noble Truths are the Buddha's first and most foundational teaching — a diagnosis of the human condition and a prescription for liberation. The first truth is dukkha: suffering and dissatisfaction exist, and even pleasant experiences are impermanent. The second truth is samudaya: suffering is caused by craving and clinging to things that cannot last. The third truth is nirodha: suffering can cease — liberation is genuinely possible if craving is let go. The fourth truth is magga: the Noble Eightfold Path is the way out of suffering. The Eightfold Path is a practical guide with eight steps, grouped into three areas. The wisdom section includes Right View and Right Intention. The ethical conduct section includes Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood. The mental training section includes Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. Together, the path addresses thought, action, and meditation as inseparable parts of living well. The ultimate goal is nirvana — the ending of craving and liberation from the cycle of samsara.

data.title: The Five Precepts, Meditation, and Community
data.sourcePassage: Buddhist ethics are grounded in the Five Precepts — voluntary guidelines to support the path to liberation. They are: not to take life, not to take what is not given, to avoid sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, and to avoid intoxicants that cloud the mind. These are not commandments from God but personal commitments to reduce harm and cultivate wisdom. Alongside ethical living, meditation is central to Buddhism. Samatha (calm-abiding) develops concentration; vipassana (insight meditation) develops wisdom about impermanence and no-self; and metta bhavana cultivates loving-kindness towards all beings. Buddhist life is lived in community. The Three Jewels — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha — are the three foundations every Buddhist takes refuge in. The Sangha includes monks, nuns, and lay practitioners who support and inspire each other. The most important Buddhist festival, Vesak, celebrates the birth, enlightenment, and death of the Buddha on the same full moon day, and is marked by temple visits, meditation, and acts of charity.
